title: Slicing Playground
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Type a row slice and a column slice for a 6 by 8 array to see which elements are selected, what shape the result has, and how a slice shares memory with the original array.

learningObjectives: Students will be able to apply `start:stop:step` slicing along both axes of a 2-D array to select a required set of elements, predict the shape of the result, and explain why changing a slice changes the original array.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Guided practice with immediate visual feedback, followed by goal-directed challenges
keyQuestions: Why is the stop value never part of the result?
What does a negative start or stop mean, and what does a negative step do?
What does it mean that a slice is a view?
commonMisconceptions: The stop index is included (the slice ends just before it).
A slice makes a copy of the data (basic slicing returns a view that shares memory with the original).
A slice that runs past the end raises an error (slices are clipped, only a single out-of-range index raises IndexError).
`a[2, :]` and `a[2:3, :]` give the same result (the first is 1-D, the second is a 2-D array with one row).
assessmentOpportunities: Given `m = np.arange(20).reshape(4, 5)` from the chapter, students write the slices that return `[[7 8 9] [12 13 14]]`, the last row reversed, and every other column, and state the shape of each result. They also explain what `m[1:3, 2:5][:] = 0` does to `m`.
